Well, the late '40s, I would say, after Pres went in the Army and he didn't come back, then we had to get musicians -- I think Basie got musicians that were more -- they could read better. 86.t: Arrangers for the Basie band and nights at the Famous Door
86.s: Dameron, Harding, Durham and Mundy wrote for the band, and the Famous Door drew stars like Ray Noble.

86.q: Well, the young arrangers began to appear on the scene like Tad Dameron, Buster Harding…then too, Don Redman used to write quite a bit for the band. And Hugo Winterhalter. But I think Buster Harding did more writing for the band and Eddie Durham used to send some arrangements to the band. But I…

86.s: Edison recommended Andy Gibson to Basie; Gibson wrote Louisiana and others.

86.t: Learning to arrange from Gus Wilson; Benny Carter

86.q: Oh, I started in the '40s. '42, '43, you know. I wrote, "Every Tug," and "I Sent for You Yesterday," "Jive at Five," that's mine. Oh, quite a few of the tunes that were recorded in those days were mine, you know.

86.t: Why arrangers from inside the band write better for it
86.s: Dance objects to albums by a single arranger; Edison says Thad Jones, Frank Wess and Frank Foster knew the band best.
86.q: So naturally, you can write for the band better than an outsider, because you're right there at all times.

251.s: The band worked as a family, splitting earnings. Cottrell, Herbert Hall, Harold Holmes and Billy Douglas wrote their own, and the first arranger in 1929 was Phil Tiller; each man wrote full scores and parts.
251.q: We didn't have any money to pay ourselves nothing. Would you have a bond for everybody in the band? Well, everybody in the band worked as a family. That's what it was. 251.q: There was five fellas in the band that arranged at one time. Harold Holmes later on when Jimmy Johnson was getting a little slow, we added Harold Holmes to the bass section. We also had a tuba, so we had a tuba, two bass fiddles in the band at the same time. Harold Holmes wrote the arrangements,…
